explanations.explanation: Jesus tells Sardis, “…you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead.” So the word around town was that this church was alive and kicking. A reputation is just what people say about you. I've seen cookies that looked perfect on the cooling rack and were still doughy inside, so I know the feeling.

Generosity never comes up in Jesus' words to Sardis. The reputation He names is being alive. Nobody in this letter is passing around a plate of anything. Jesus says He knows their deeds, and then He names what they're known for.
Money isn't mentioned anywhere in this letter to Sardis. Jesus says they have “…a reputation for being alive…” That's the thing people said about them. Nobody is counting coins here, friend.

That's the word Jesus uses: “…you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead.” That's a hard sentence to hear. I think it's also why the next thing He says is “Wake up.” He's speaking straight to them, and He isn't done with them yet.

Jesus never calls Sardis proud. He says they have a reputation for being alive, “yet you are dead.” Pride is a fine guess, since a good reputation can go to your head. But the text only gives us the one word, and it's dead.

Poor isn't the word Jesus uses for Sardis. What He says is “…you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead.” He's talking about how they look next to how they really are. So the word to hold onto is dead.

Jesus says, “Wake up and strengthen what remains, which is about to die…” Wake up comes first. After that comes the work of strengthening what's left. A church called dead gets an alarm clock before it gets anything else.

Jesus never tells Sardis to leave town. He says, “Wake up and strengthen what remains…” He's talking to the church right where it is. The job is waking up and strengthening what's left, and it happens in Sardis.

Rest is the opposite of what Jesus asks. He says, “Wake up and strengthen what remains, which is about to die…” A church that's dead to begin with doesn't need a nap. I know a nap sounds good, I really do, but here the word is wake.

Half of it is right. Jesus does say to strengthen what remains, which is about to die. But then He says, “…I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God.” So He says incomplete, not complete.

Jesus says, “…I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God.” He doesn't say complete. The first part is true: He tells them to strengthen what remains, which is about to die. So this one is half true and half not.

It's the other way around. Jesus says, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you.” Not waking up means they won't know the hour. A thief doesn't call ahead, friend.

Jesus says, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief, and you will not know the hour when I will come upon you.” So they will not know the hour. That's why waking up matters. This is also why I keep my ovens ready, because no one knows the day (Matthew 24:36).

Jesus says, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief…” A thief doesn't send a text first. That's the point of the picture, because the hour isn't known. It's a warning, and it comes with a way to be ready: wake up.
Jesus doesn't say a storm. He says, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief…” A storm at least has clouds you can see coming. A thief comes without you knowing the hour.
A king is a good guess, but it isn't the picture Jesus uses here. He says, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief…” He's talking about not knowing the hour. So the comparison is the thief.

Jesus says, “But you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and because they are worthy, they will walk with Me in white.” Even in a church called dead, He sees these few. He hasn't missed a single one of them. Walking with Him is the promise.

Jesus does say it. “But you do have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their garments, and because they are worthy, they will walk with Me in white.” Those few are named right there in the letter. They get to walk with Him.
Jesus says, “And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life…” That's a promise to the one who overcomes. Never means never. I'd hold onto that one tight.

Jesus says the opposite. “And I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life, but I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.” The promise is for the one who overcomes. His name stays.
Jesus says, “…I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.” He says the overcomer's name out loud in front of them. That's a name worth being known by.

Those two groups are not who Jesus names here. He says, “…I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.” His Father and the angels are the ones who hear it. It's a good guess, but the text gives a different list.

Jesus doesn't name the kings of the earth here. He says, “…I will confess his name before My Father and His angels.” The ones who hear it are His Father and the angels. No crowns needed for that audience, friend.

Jesus says, “What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.” That's a lot of power in a single key. Nobody can slam what He opens. I had a lot of drawers closed on me in my day, so I notice that line.

Priests aren't mentioned in this verse. Jesus says, “What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.” The focus is on who holds the key, not on who walks through. So the answer is that no one can shut what He opens.
That's not what Jesus says. He says, “What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.” Nobody is closing up for the night. What He opens stays open.
Jesus says, “Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut.” It matches what He said about the key. He opens it, and no one can shut it. It's placed right in front of them.

Jesus doesn't set a burden in front of Philadelphia. He says, “Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut.” A door is something you can walk through. So the answer is the open door.

A wall is the opposite of what Jesus puts there. He says, “Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut.” Walls keep you out, but this is an open door. And with that key, no one can shut it.

Jesus says, “I know that you have only a little strength…” So the church in Philadelphia doesn't have great strength. But He goes on to say they have kept His word and have not denied His name. A little strength can still do a lot.

Jesus says, “I know that you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name.” So it's a little strength, not great strength. The yet in that sentence matters, because they still kept His word. Small can still be faithful.
Jesus says, “…you have kept My word and have not denied My name.” They had only a little strength and still didn't deny Him. That's a church I'd want in my bakery line.
Spoken isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “…you have kept My word and have not denied My name.” The word is denied. They kept His word and did not deny His name.
Praised isn't the word in the verse. Jesus says, “…you have kept My word and have not denied My name.” What they did not do is deny it. They did that even with only a little strength.

It's flipped around. Jesus says He will make those who claim to be Jews but are liars “…come and bow down at your feet…” They come to Philadelphia's feet, not the other way. And then “…they will know that I love you.”

Jesus says, “I will make them come and bow down at your feet, and they will know that I love you.” The liars bow at the feet of the church in Philadelphia. The church isn't made to bow to them. And the point is that they will know He loves the church.

Jesus says, “…and they will know that I love you.” That's the end of the sentence, and it's the heart of it. To a church with only a little strength, He says He loves them. I can't think of a better word to end on.
Warns isn't the word in this verse. Jesus says, “…and they will know that I love you.” What they will know is His love for the church in Philadelphia. So the word is loves.
Tests isn't what Jesus says here. He says, “…and they will know that I love you.” Testing does come up in the next verse, but that's about the hour of testing. Here the word is loves.

Jesus says, “Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world…” The because is right there in the verse. They kept His command, and He will keep them. That's a promise from Him.

Jesus does say it. “Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.” He ties it to their keeping His command to persevere. So the answer is true.

explanations.answer: So no one will take their crown
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “I am coming soon. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.” The crown is the reason He gives. They're to hold on to what they have. That's the whole reason, plain as day.

explanations.answer: So the open door won't close
explanations.explanation: It's a smart guess, but Jesus already said no one can shut that door. The reason He gives here is, “…so that no one will take your crown.” He says to hold fast to what they have for that reason. The door isn't the worry in this verse.
Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.” The reason is the crown. Growing strength isn't named in the verse.

Jesus says, “…and the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God)…” The text names the city for us. It comes down out of heaven from His God. And the overcomer gets that name written on him.

Philadelphia is the church's own city, but it isn't the city Jesus names. He says, “…the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God)…” That city comes down out of heaven. So the answer is the new Jerusalem.

Bethlehem is the town where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), but it's not the city here. Jesus says, “…the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God)…” That's the city named in the verse.

Jesus says, “Upon him I will write the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God… and My new name.” So there are three names in all. His own new name is the last one. It's written on the one who overcomes.
Jesus does say it. “Upon him I will write the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God… and My new name.” His new name is the third one on the list. So the answer is true.
